metadata.hardware_requirements: NVIDIA Quadro K620 GPU and Intel Xeon CPU E5-1650 (3.6 GHz, 6 cores)

nodes_source.source_quote: A series of simulation experiments based on real-world traffic data are conducted to evaluate the proposed approach.
nodes_source.description: Traffic data from a real-world setting, used as the basis for simulation experiments to evaluate the DRL approach.
nodes_source.reproducibility_rationale: Access 'upon request' from authors, no public link or DOI.

nodes_source.source_quote: Instead, it uses traffic video frames as inputs and learns the optimal control strategies directly from high-dimensional visual inputs...
nodes_source.description: Visual inputs derived from traffic video data, preprocessed (zoomed and down-sampled) into position matrices, used as direct inputs to the DRL model.
nodes_source.reproducibility_rationale: Implied 'upon request' from authors, no public link or DOI for this specific form of data.

nodes_source.source_quote: Wattleworth [10] firstly formulated a linear programming model to optimize a fixed signal timing plan for ramp metering based on historical traffic volume data.
nodes_source.description: Traffic volume data used by Wattleworth [10] to optimize fixed signal timing plans for ramp metering, not directly used in this paper's methodology.
nodes_source.reproducibility_rationale: Cited reference only [10], no URL or repository for the data itself.

nodes_process.source_quote: We propose a deep reinforcement learning (DRL) method to explore the potential of traffic video data in improving the efficiency of ramp metering.
nodes_process.description: A deep reinforcement learning (DRL) method is proposed for local ramp metering using traffic video data. It adopts a two-phase control scheme where a policy determines if the next phase is green or red at a fixed time step L based on the current traffic state.

nodes_process.node_name: Extract Vehicle Locations to Position Matrices
nodes_process.source_quote: Vehicle locations are extracted from the traffic video frames and are reformed as position matrices.
nodes_process.description: Vehicle locations are extracted from raw traffic video frames and then reformed into position matrices. A vehicle is represented by a location point (x, y_i).
nodes_process.reproducibility_rationale: clarity=2, no specific extraction algorithm stated.

nodes_process.node_name: Stack Position Matrices for State Representation
nodes_process.source_quote: Since one matrix is insufficient to describe vehicle dynamics, we stack the matrices of consecutive N time steps to represent the state s_t: S_t = {m_{t-(N-1)},..., m_t}.
nodes_process.description: To capture vehicle dynamics, position matrices from N consecutive time steps are stacked to form the traffic state representation S_t.

nodes_process.source_quote: For computation efficiency, down-sampling is introduced before the matrix stack to reduce the input dimensions and maintain sufficient information about vehicle positions.
nodes_process.description: Down-sampling is applied to the position matrices before stacking to reduce input dimensions and improve computational efficiency while retaining vehicle position information. The target size of one observation after down-sampling is 4x512 pixels.
nodes_process.reproducibility_rationale: clarity=2, target size stated, but downsampling method unclear.

nodes_process.source_quote: The reward r_t after action a_t is defined by the following: r_t = mu*v_t + omega*q_t, mu > 0, omega < 0
nodes_process.description: The reward function r_t is defined as a linear combination of the average speed in the merging area (v_t) and the average queue length at the on-ramp (q_t), with positive weight mu and negative weight omega.

nodes_process.source_quote: We adopt a deep neural network termed Q-network to approximate Q*(s, a). The neural network contains several convolutional layers and fully connected layers.
nodes_process.description: A deep neural network, termed Q-network, is adopted to approximate the optimal action-value function Q*(s, a). This network includes convolutional layers for feature extraction and fully connected layers for Q-value estimation.

nodes_process.source_quote: the Q-network in Mnih et al. [30] is revised as Figure 7, which consists of three convolutional neural network (CNN) layers and one full connection (FC) layer for each output layer.
nodes_process.description: The Q-network architecture is a revision of Mnih et al. [30], consisting of three convolutional neural network (CNN) layers and one fully connected (FC) layer for each output layer. It has approximately 2 million weights.
nodes_process.reproducibility_rationale: clarity=4, all params stated, but generic tools only.

nodes_process.source_quote: The gradient-based algorithm Adam [28] is used to update w_i to minimize the loss function.
nodes_process.description: The Adam optimization algorithm is used to update the weights w_i of the Q-network, minimizing the defined loss function.

nodes_process.source_quote: The experience replay [30] stores the data prepared for training into the replay buffer and samples these data uniformly for training the agent.
nodes_process.description: Experience replay is implemented to store training data in a replay buffer and then uniformly sample from it. This makes the training data independently and identically distributed, stabilizing training.

nodes_process.source_quote: The target network [29] is introduced for a stable estimation of target value Q*(s, a). When Q-network is being trained, the target network is freezing. Its parameters w- are updated by copying w_i in Q-network with a certain frequency.
nodes_process.description: A target network is introduced to provide a stable estimate of the target Q-value. Its parameters are periodically updated by copying the weights from the main Q-network at a specified frequency (freeze interval).

nodes_process.node_name: Implement Multitask Learning and Loss Function
nodes_process.source_quote: A multitask learning strategy is implemented in the training process to improve learning efficiency. While training the ramp metering Q-network, the mean speed in the merging area and the queue length at the on-ramp are predicted simultaneously.
nodes_process.description: A multitask learning strategy is implemented to simultaneously predict mean speed and queue length alongside the Q-value. The total loss function combines the Q-learning loss (L1) and a prediction accuracy loss (L2) with a weight (lambda).
nodes_process.reproducibility_rationale: clarity=4, 0/1 tool named, all params stated.

nodes_process.source_quote: The algorithm for training the ramp metering policy is presented in Algorithm 1. The ramp meter takes new action with the e-greedy strategy, meaning that the agent does not always adopt the best action derived from current Q (s, a, w).
nodes_process.description: The deep Q-learning agent is trained using an epsilon-greedy strategy for action selection, balancing exploration and exploitation. Training is performed over 1 million frames.
nodes_process.reproducibility_rationale: clarity=4, 0/1 tool named, all params stated.

nodes_process.source_quote: The proposed method is evaluated in SUMO, an open-source microscopic traffic simulator [31]. The simulation is performed in the freeway connecting Qingdao and Huangdao through a tunnel in Shandong, China, as shown in Figure 5.
nodes_process.description: The proposed DRL method is evaluated using SUMO, an open-source microscopic traffic simulator. The simulation environment models a freeway connecting Qingdao and Huangdao, including a one-lane on-ramp and a three-lane mainline.
parameters_mentioned: road_network_configuration=one-lane on-ramp, upstream three-lane mainline, freeway reduces to three lanes downstream

nodes_process.source_quote: Figure 6 presents the 10-min traffic volumes from 7:50 a.m. to 9:00 a.m. in the mainline and at the on-ramp.
nodes_process.description: Traffic volumes for the mainline and on-ramp are collected in 10-minute intervals from 7:50 a.m. to 9:00 a.m. within the simulation environment.

nodes_process.source_quote: The simulation considers the road network covering the on-ramp, the upstream and downstream mainlines, and the merging area.
nodes_process.description: Simulation experiments are conducted using the trained DRL agent within the SUMO environment to evaluate its performance on the defined road network. Experiments are initialized with different random seeds.

nodes_process.source_quote: The first scenario does not apply ramp metering
nodes_process.description: A baseline scenario is simulated where no ramp metering control is applied to the traffic system to serve as a comparison.

nodes_process.source_quote: the second scenario adopts the PI-ALINEA method. The PI-ALINEA method fixes the length of the green phase and determines the length of the red phase in the current signal cycle based on the length of the red phase in the previous cycle and the downstream occupancies in the previous and current cycles.
nodes_process.description: A baseline scenario is simulated using the PI-ALINEA ramp metering method. This method fixes the green phase length and determines the red phase length based on previous red phase length and downstream occupancies.
nodes_process.reproducibility_rationale: clarity=3, 0/1 tool named, all params stated.

nodes_process.source_quote: The results demonstrate that, in comparison with a state-of-the-practice method, the proposed DRL method results in (1) lower travel times in the mainline
nodes_process.description: Mainline travel times are evaluated and compared across the DRL, PI-ALINEA, and no-control scenarios to assess the DRL method's performance.

nodes_process.source_quote: the proposed DRL method results in (2) shorter vehicle queues at the on-ramp
nodes_process.description: Vehicle queue lengths at the on-ramp are evaluated and compared across the DRL, PI-ALINEA, and no-control scenarios.

nodes_process.source_quote: the proposed DRL method results in (3) higher traffic flows downstream of the merging area.
nodes_process.description: Traffic flows downstream of the merging area are evaluated and compared across the DRL, PI-ALINEA, and no-control scenarios.

nodes_process.source_quote: Figure 10 presents the temporal-spatial distribution of the mean speeds along the mainline. The results further demonstrate the efficiency of the ramp metering and the better performance of the proposed method.
nodes_process.description: The temporal-spatial distribution of mean speeds along the mainline is analyzed for each scenario (no-control, PI-ALINEA, DRL) to demonstrate ramp metering efficiency.

nodes_process.node_name: Analyze Queue Length and Red Ratio
nodes_process.source_quote: Figure 12 presents the mean queue lengths at the on-ramp and the red ratios (i.e., the proportion of the red phase in the simulation time) in each simulation for the two ramp metering methods.
nodes_process.description: The relationship between mean queue lengths at the on-ramp and red ratios (proportion of red phase in simulation time) is analyzed for the DRL and PI-ALINEA methods.

nodes_process.source_quote: Figure 13 presents the queue lengths at the on-ramp and the occupancy downstream of the merging area for the two ramp metering methods.
nodes_process.description: The relationship between queue lengths at the on-ramp and occupancy downstream of the merging area is analyzed for the DRL and PI-ALINEA methods.

nodes_process.source_quote: A perturbation analysis is conducted to evaluate the impact of information contained in video data. As shown in Figure 15, the control area is divided into eight subareas. The sensors applied in PI-ALINEA are located in subarea 2. The information in the subarea is removed from original data to generate perturbed data for each subarea.
nodes_process.description: A perturbation analysis is conducted by dividing the control area into eight subareas. Information is removed from each subarea (including subarea 2, where PI-ALINEA sensors are located) from original data to generate perturbed data.
nodes_process.reproducibility_rationale: clarity=3, method of removal not fully specified.

nodes_process.node_name: Evaluate Travel Time with Perturbed Data
nodes_process.source_quote: missing information for each subarea is evaluated in 20 simulation experiments with perturbed data. Figure 16 presents the box plot of travel time when the information of different subareas is removed, and the baseline is the result of experiments that take original data as input.
nodes_process.description: Travel times are evaluated in 20 simulation experiments using the perturbed data from each subarea. Results are compared against a baseline using original data to assess the impact of missing information.
